steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on DoCo, a contrastive pre-training method that improves visual document understanding in large visual-language models. Cover the move from LLMs to LVLMs, why current LVLMs struggle with text-rich images, how DoCo works, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs and their extension to vision (LVLMs)
2. LVLMs in text-rich scenarios / visual document understanding, and the fine-grained collapse problem
3. DoCo: document object contrastive learning
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs -> LVLMs
- LLMs: strong text generation and understanding; aligned with user intent via instruction fine-tuning; interactive, productivity-boosting assistants
- limitation: text only, no images, speech, video -> curtails applicability
- LVLMs devised to let LLMs perceive and understand visual signals; potential on real-world visual challenges

2. Text-rich scenarios
- proficiency in visual document understanding (VDU) limited, insufficient specific training
- recent LVLMs for VDU: large-scale document data or multiple VDU tasks
  - mPLUG-DocOwl: comprehensive dataset for document image comprehension
  - LLaVAR: text recognition pre-training task for text-rich images
  - UniDoc: unified multimodal instruction tuning on large-scale instruction following datasets
- still struggle to capture textual details in images
- Fig. 1 (a): vision encoders initialized from CLIP-based weights; contrastive, image-level instance discrimination
- image-level representations not optimal for dense prediction like VDU; miss fine-grained features
- question: can fine-grained features improve LVLMs in text-rich scenarios? -> fine-grained collapse issue, lacks investigation

3. DoCo (Fig. 1 (b))
- multimodal encoder: visual, layout, textual features of document objects; aligned to visual features of LVLM image encoder
- pre-training: image encoder turns whole image into embeddings, consistent with LVLM visual feature extraction
- layout + textual contents of document objects from OCR engine -> multimodal encoder
- outputs of two encoders aligned contrastively
- image encoder gets more effective visual cues from document objects
- plug-and-play; various LVLMs; no extra computational complexity at inference

4. Contributions
- importance of fine-grained features in VDU; fine-grained feature collapse issue; first to research enhancing visual information for LVLMs
- DoCo contrastive framework for better visual features and perception of document objects
- experiments on various VDU datasets: significant improvements

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted more and more research interest because of their powerful capabilities in text generation and understanding. These models can be aligned with the intent of users by fine-tuning on instructions, and they show strong interactive capabilities and the potential to be intelligent assistants that boost productivity. However these models are inherently limited to textual data, and they cannot process other common modalities like images, speech and video. This curtails the applicability of these models a lot. To get around this constraint, a set of Large Visual-Language Models (LVLMs) has been devised so that LLMs can perceive and understand visual signals. These LVLMs have shown a lot of potential for real-world visual challenges.

These multimodal large models have good capabilities in multimodal understanding, but they are still limited in text-rich scenarios, such as visual document understanding (VDU) tasks, because they lack specific training. To address this, recent work on LVLMs has explored VDU performance further, either by training with large-scale document data or by combining multiple VDU tasks of multimodal understanding. For example, mPLUG-DocOwl builds a comprehensive dataset for document image comprehension. LLaVAR adds a text recognition pre-training task to improve the understanding of text-rich images. UniDoc does unified multimodal instruction tuning on large-scale instruction following datasets that it contributes. These works have made significant progress in text-rich scenarios, but they still have trouble capturing the textual details inside images accurately. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), the vision encoders of these models are initialized from CLIP-based weights, which are pre-trained with contrastive learning to align visual and textual inputs across modalities through image-level instance discrimination. But these image-level representations are not optimal for dense prediction tasks like VDU, and they do not extract fine-grained visual features. This leads to a question: how can exploring fine-grained features improve the performance of LVLMs in text-rich scenarios? We call this the fine-grained collapse issue, and it has not been investigated much in the VDU field.

- DoCo (Fig. 1 (b)): multimodal encoder gets visual, layout and textual features of document objects; aligned to visual features of LVLM image encoder
- pre-training: image encoder embeds whole image like LVLMs do; layout + text from OCR engine into multimodal encoder; two encoders' outputs aligned contrastively
- image encoder gets better visual cues from document objects -> better understanding of text-rich scenarios
- plug-and-play, works for various LVLMs, no extra computational complexity at inference

- contributions: fine-grained feature collapse issue (first to research enhancing visual info for LVLMs); DoCo framework; significant gains on various VDU datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted more and more research interest because of their powerful capabilities in text generation and understanding. These models can be aligned with the intent of users by fine-tuning on instructions, and they show strong interactive capabilities and the potential to be intelligent assistants that boost productivity. However these models are inherently limited to textual data, and they cannot process other common modalities like images, speech and video. This curtails the applicability of these models a lot. To get around this constraint, a set of Large Visual-Language Models (LVLMs) has been devised so that LLMs can perceive and understand visual signals. These LVLMs have shown a lot of potential for real-world visual challenges.

These multimodal large models have good capabilities in multimodal understanding, but they are still limited in text-rich scenarios, such as visual document understanding (VDU) tasks, because they lack specific training. To address this, recent work on LVLMs has explored VDU performance further, either by training with large-scale document data or by combining multiple VDU tasks of multimodal understanding. For example, mPLUG-DocOwl builds a comprehensive dataset for document image comprehension. LLaVAR adds a text recognition pre-training task to improve the understanding of text-rich images. UniDoc does unified multimodal instruction tuning on large-scale instruction following datasets that it contributes. These works have made significant progress in text-rich scenarios, but they still have trouble capturing the textual details inside images accurately. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), the vision encoders of these models are initialized from CLIP-based weights, which are pre-trained with contrastive learning to align visual and textual inputs across modalities through image-level instance discrimination. But these image-level representations are not optimal for dense prediction tasks like VDU, and they do not extract fine-grained visual features. This leads to a question: how can exploring fine-grained features improve the performance of LVLMs in text-rich scenarios? We call this the fine-grained collapse issue, and it has not been investigated much in the VDU field.

In this work we introduce a new Document Object COntrastive learning (DoCo) method for this problem, shown in Fig. 1 (b). We use a contrastive learning approach where a multimodal encoder obtains the multimodal features (i.e. visual, layout and textual) of document objects, and these are aligned to the visual features that the image encoder of the LVLM produces. In the pre-training phase, the image encoder processes the whole image into a series of embeddings, in the same way as the visual feature extraction of LVLMs. Besides the visual features, the layout information and the textual contents of the document objects, which come from the OCR engine, are embedded into the multimodal encoder to capture the fine-grained features. Then the output representations of the two encoders are trained to align with contrastive learning. This way the image encoder of LVLMs can get more effective visual cues from the document objects, and the understanding of text-rich scenarios gets stronger. DoCo is a plug-and-play pre-training method, so it can be used in the pre-training of various LVLMs and it does not increase computational complexity during inference. Our main contributions are three:

- We look at the importance of fine-grained features in VDU tasks and propose the fine-grained feature collapse issue. As far as we know, we are the first to research enhancing visual information for LVLMs.

- We propose DoCo for the fine-grained feature collapse issue. It is a contrastive learning framework that helps LVLMs get more useful visual features in text-rich scenarios and improves the perception of document objects.

- Experiments on various VDU datasets show that our method gives significant performance improvements for LVLMs in text-rich scenes.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) [1,2,3,4,5] have aroused increasing research interest due to their powerful text generation and understanding capabilities. These models can be aligned with user intent through instruction fine-tuning, demonstrating strong interactive capabilities and the potential to serve as productivity-boosting intelligent assistants. However, these models are inherently confined to the domain of textual data, and are incapable of processing other prevalent modalities such as images, speech, and video, which significantly curtails their applicability. To circumvent this constraint, a set of Large Visual-Language Models (LVLMs) [6,7,8,9,10] has been devised to enhance the ability of LLMs to perceive and understand visual signals, showing immense potential in addressing real-world visual challenges.

Despite their commendable capabilities in multimodal understanding, these multimodal large models remain limited in text-rich scenarios, such as visual document understanding (VDU) tasks, due to insufficient specific training. To address this issue, recent advancements in LVLMs [11,12,13,14] have further explored VDU performance, utilizing large-scale document data for training or combining multiple VDU tasks of multimodal understanding. For example, mPLUG-DocOwl [11] constructs a comprehensive dataset dedicated to document image comprehension. LLaVAR [12] incorporates a text recognition pre-training task to enhance the understanding of text-rich images. UniDoc [13] implements unified multimodal instruction tuning on its contributed large-scale instruction following datasets. While these works have made significant strides in text-rich scenarios, they still struggle to accurately capture the textual details within images. As depicted in Fig. 1 (a), the vision encoders of these models are initialized from CLIP-based [15] weights, which are pre-trained through contrastive learning to foster cross-modality alignment between visual and textual inputs via image-level instance discrimination. Such image-level representations, however, are not optimal for dense prediction tasks such as VDU and fail to extract fine-grained visual features. This leads to the following question: how can the exploration of fine-grained features enhance the performance of LVLMs in text-rich scenarios? We define this as the fine-grained collapse issue, which still lacks investigation in the VDU field.

In this work, we introduce a novel Document Object COntrastive learning (DoCo) approach tailored to this problem, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (b). Concretely, we adopt contrastive learning, leveraging a multimodal encoder to obtain the multimodal features (i.e., visual, layout and textual) of document objects and aligning them to the visual features produced by the image encoder of the LVLM. During pre-training, the image encoder processes the whole image into a series of embeddings, consistent with the visual feature extraction of LVLMs. Beyond visual features, the layout information and textual contents of the document objects derived from the OCR engine are embedded by the multimodal encoder to capture fine-grained features. The output representations of the two encoders are then trained to align in a contrastive manner. In this way, the image encoder of LVLMs can acquire more effective visual cues from the document objects, strengthening the understanding of text-rich scenarios. Note that DoCo is a plug-and-play pre-training method, which can be applied in the pre-training of various LVLMs without any increase in computational complexity during inference. To sum up, our main contributions are threefold:

- We investigate the importance of fine-grained features in VDU tasks and propose the fine-grained feature collapse issue. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to research the enhancement of visual information for LVLMs.

- We propose DoCo, tailored to the fine-grained feature collapse issue, which introduces a contrastive learning framework to help LVLMs acquire more beneficial visual features in text-rich scenarios and enhance the perception of document objects.

- Experimental results on various VDU datasets demonstrate that our method brings significant performance improvements for LVLMs in text-rich scenes.
